title: Looking back: the Dhammapada

lines: A BOOKMARK STUCK AT PAGE FORTY.
cards: Most people have started a big book and never finished it. It sits on the nightstand with a bookmark stuck at page forty, quietly judging.
This year you did something a lot of people never do: you read a whole book of scripture, cover to cover, a few verses at a time, over seventy-five days.
At the end, you picked ten verses that stayed with you and wrote them down. Somewhere, maybe on a scrap of paper or in your phone, those ten are waiting.

teach.b: The Dhammapada: the path of the teaching, or the verses of the teaching.

Four hundred twenty-three verses in twenty-six chapters, the best-loved book of the Buddha's sayings across the Theravada world, carried across Asia in several languages, and brought into English by Max Müller in the nineteenth century.

teach.h: ALL THAT WE ARE — THE TWIN VERSES.
teach.b: You began with the twin verses. In Müller's translation, the very first line is: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought."
A few verses later came the one many people remember first: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." Then the chapters rolled on. Earnestness.
Thought, and the body fragile as a jar. Flowers. The fool and the wise.
The thousands, where conquering yourself beats conquering a thousand thousand men.

teach.h: DROP BY DROP, CHAPTER BY CHAPTER.
teach.b: Evil and good, filling the water-pot drop by drop. Old age. Self.
The Buddha, whose teaching fits in one line: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. Happiness, where contentment is the greatest wealth. Anger.
Other people's faults, so easy to see. The way. The elephant.
Thirst, and the best gift, the gift of the teaching. And at the end, the mendicant and the brahmana, the one who is truly worthy.
A verse you read months ago may mean something different now. Not because the verse changed. You did.
That's why people keep this book for a lifetime: not to finish it, but to come back. Twenty-six chapters, read whole.

how: Buddhists across the Theravada world memorize and recite verses of the Dhammapada, hear them in sermons, and teach them to children; many keep a copy for a lifetime and return to favorite verses.

o: coming back to verses that mean more now

only monks need to read it twice.
games.why: people keep this book for a lifetime, not to finish it but to come back: the same verse meets a different you.

practice: Find your ten verses, on paper or in your phone, and read them slowly, once; if you can't find them, let one you remember come to mind. Notice which verse lands differently now than when you first wrote it down.
Then set the words aside and simply sit.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. The Dhammapada: four hundred twenty-three verses, twenty-six chapters, read whole, and ten of them yours.

orig.note: Pali dhammapada: dhamma (the teaching) + pada (path, step, verse): the path of the teaching, or its verses.

carryVoice: Your line: the verses stay. The same verse can meet a different you. See you tomorrow.
